shower.thought: We spend our entire lives learning how to be human, but we never get to see if we passed.
Your phone knows more about your daily patterns than you do.
The only time you ever see your face is when you're looking at a reflection or a photo — never the way others see it.
If you can imagine it, someone somewhere is probably doing it right now.
You've never actually touched anything in your life — just the electromagnetic force fields around atoms.
The things you regret most are usually the moments you acted exactly like yourself.
Every song you love is just someone else's diary that happened to match your mood.
You can't think about not thinking about something without thinking about it.
Time moves faster the less you're paying attention to it, which might be why childhood takes forever.
Your laugh is the only sound you make that you've never actually heard the way others hear it.
Most of what you know about yourself comes from stories you've told so many times you believe them as fact.
The moment you become aware of your breathing, you have to manually control it until you forget again.
People spend years trying to forget their trauma while simultaneously making sure they never forget the lesson — which might be the same thing.
Your skeleton has been inside you the whole time, holding everything together, and you never think about it.
The last time you did something for the first time is already behind you, and you didn't even know it was the last time.
You are statistically closer to being dead than being born.
The worst version of yourself is the one that exists only in your head as a possibility.
If a tree falls in the forest with no one around, it makes a sound — your brain just wouldn't register it as real.
You've probably forgotten more than you'll ever remember, and that forgetting might be more important than the remembering.
Every embarrassing moment you remember, the other person has probably forgotten.

darkjoke.thought:
My grandfather said, "Your generation is too reliant on technology."
I said, "You're right," and unplugged his life support.

I told my friend he was being paranoid about his girlfriend cheating.
He said, "Am I though?" while showing me her location was at his brother's apartment.
I said, "Yes, definitely paranoid." I'm a good friend.

My therapist asked why I never finish anything.
I said—
I've been trying to adult, but apparently I'm still in the trial period and customer service won't call me back.

My boss asked if I had any weaknesses during the interview.
I said, "I'm a perfectionist."
He hired me on the spot.
Three years later, I'm pretty sure he knows the real answer now.

I asked my wife why she married me if I annoyed her so much.
She said, "I didn't know yet."
At least she's honest.

The doctor told me I had six months to live.
I couldn't pay the bill.
He said, "Okay, you've got a year."

My kid asked me why I was sad.
I said, "Because the world is cruel and meaningless."
He said, "No, I meant why are you sad about the show you're watching?"
I forgot which one was which.

People keep asking if I'm okay because I've been quiet lately.
No, I'm planning.

My wife accused me of never remembering our anniversary.
I said, "That's not true. I remember it perfectly—it's just that I don't care."
Honesty was apparently not the policy here.

I told my son that when he was born, it was the happiest day of my life.
He asked what changed.
I said, "About five minutes, really."

My therapist said I'm deflecting with humor.
I said, "That's ridiculous," then laughed for forty-five minutes.

I ran into my ex at the grocery store.
She said she'd been meaning to call me.
I said, "Let's not ruin the good memory we have."
We both knew the good memory was breaking up.

My mother asked why I never visit.
I said, "Because you're always home."

I've made peace with my mortality.
Mostly because I ran out of other options.

I told my son life gets easier with age.
He asked, "When does that start?"
I'm still waiting for an answer.

My wife asked if I loved her more than my job.
I quit the next day.
Best decision I ever made—turns out I hate being unemployed way less than being married.

I tried to make a joke about my anxiety.
But I was too worried it wouldn't land.

My friend said he was going through an existential crisis.
I told him, "Just wait, it gets worse."
He appreciated the honesty more than the support.

The hardest part about growing old isn't the aches and pains.
It's realizing all those people who said I'd understand things better someday were completely right, and that's depressing.
